title: Proudhon, Blanqui and the Early Workers' Movements

cards.b: Before 1848 the workers' movement had three tendencies: mutual aid and anti-statism (Proudhon), conspiratorial insurrection (Blanqui), and the democratic, mass-organising Chartists. Marx fought and borrowed from all three. Their arguments about reform, revolution and the party come back through the rest of this course.

After 1815, craftsmen and mill workers formed mutual societies, secret clubs and unions, often illegal. Combination laws in Britain were repealed in 1824. The Lyon silk-weavers (canuts) rose in 1831 and 1834. In Britain, the People's Charter (1838) demanded votes for all men, secret ballot and pay for MPs. In Europe, 1848 was the year of revolutions.

Pierre-Joseph Proudhon (1809-65), a printer from Besançon, wrote What Is Property? (1840): "property is theft", meaning unearned income from ownership. He wanted free credit through a People's Bank, mutual exchange among small producers and federation instead of state power. In System of Economic Contradictions (1846) he claimed to show the philosophy of poverty. He called himself an anarchist, the first to do so positively.

Marx answered with The Poverty of Philosophy (1847), a pun on Proudhon's subtitle. He charged that Proudhon wanted to keep commodity production and money while removing their effects, and that categories like "justice" ignored history. Yet Proudhon's federal, small-scale ideas lived on in the First International and in the Paris Commune (1871).

Louis Auguste Blanqui (1805-81) spent roughly half his adult life in prison. He believed a small, disciplined secret society could seize power in Paris and rule temporarily on behalf of the people (a "dictatorship"). Blanqui's tactics stressed conspiracy, not mass organisation. Lenin later admired his determination while insisting on a party rooted in the working class.

cards.h: Chartists, Louis Blanc and the national workshops
cards.b: Chartists mixed petitions, strikes and mass meetings. Their 1839, 1842 and 1848 petitions all failed in Parliament. Louis Blanc (The Organisation of Labour, 1839) proposed state-backed workshops and the slogan "from each according to his abilities, to each according to his needs." In 1848 the Paris national workshops, a pale version of his plan, closed in June; the workers' rising was crushed by General Cavaignac with several thousand killed.

The Manifesto (written for the Communist League, published February 1848) met a continent in revolt. The upheavals produced republics, then reaction. Marx concluded that workers must organise independently of middle-class liberals and that state power was the central prize. Engels later said barricade tactics were obsolete as armies modernised.

The First International (1864), with Marx as leading organiser, brought Proudhonists, trade unionists and Blanquists into one body, until it split in 1872.

cards.h: What the early movements got wrong, or right
cards.b:
Marx on Proudhon: a petty-bourgeois dreamer. Anarchists: Marx's centralism threatened freedom, a charge Bakunin pressed. Liberals: Blanqui's minority rule shows the authoritarian risk of "revolution on behalf of the people".

Historians: Proudhon was no feminist: he defended patriarchal family hierarchy and held racist and antisemitic views, a stain on his legacy. Chartism failed to win its six points by 1848, though almost all but annual parliaments were enacted later.

Early Indian labour organising echoed these arguments: Narayan Meghaji Lokhande set up the Bombay Millhands' Association (1890); N.M. Joshi and the AITUC (1920) followed the British trade-union model. M.N. Roy's generation read Blanquist-style insurrection in the Kanpur and Meerut conspiracy cases (1924, 1929). The Gandhian cooperative-and-village idea has Proudhonian overtones of small producers, mutual aid and decentralisation, though Gandhi never read him closely.

Key takeaways

  1. Proudhon: property is theft, mutual exchange and federation.
  2. Blanqui: insurrection by a disciplined minority.
  3. Chartists and Louis Blanc: mass pressure and state-backed labour.
  4. 1848 taught Marx that workers must act as an independent class.
  5. Anarchist and liberal critics saw authoritarian risks in both centralism and conspiracy.

Debate questions

  1. Is a small disciplined minority ever a legitimate vehicle for revolution?
  2. Would a Proudhon-style economy of small producers work in a modern industrial society?
